title: Intraoperative Miotics: Precision Pupillary Control
summary: A comprehensive guide to the pharmacologic agents used to induce miosis during intraocular surgery. Mastering these agents is critical for IOL stabilization, penetrating keratoplasty, and managing complex anterior segment procedures.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Intraoperative miotics are parasympathomimetic agents injected directly into the anterior chamber (AC) to induce rapid constriction of the iris sphincter muscle. They are primarily utilized to stabilize Intraocular Lenses (IOLs), protect the crystalline lens or IOL during surgical maneuvers, and lower immediate postoperative intraocular pressure (IOP).

sections.title: Primary Indications
content: Phacoemulsification: To ensure IOL centration and prevent iris incarceration.
Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP): To protect the host iris and the underlying lens/IOL.
Glaucoma Surgery: To pull iris tissue away from the angle during trabeculectomy.
Anterior Vitrectomy: To constrict the pupil and sequester vitreous in the posterior segment.
Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI): Pre-treatment to thin the peripheral iris (topical).

sections.title: Miochol-E Reconstitution Process
content: Step 1: Inspect the Univial dual-chamber container for clarity.
Step 2: Press the plastic plunger to dislodge the rubber stopper between chambers.
Step 3: Shake gently to mix the lyophilized Acetylcholine powder with the electrolyte diluent.
Step 4: Draw the 1:100 solution into a sterile syringe using a filtered needle.
Step 5: Administer into the AC within 6 hours of preparation.

sections.title: Surgical Administration Technique
content: Step 1: Evacuate Ophthalmic Viscosurgical Device (OVD) from the AC.
Step 2: Introduce a 27G or 30G blunt-tipped cannula through the side-port incision.
Step 3: Gently irrigate the miotic agent over the iris surface or behind the IOL.
Step 4: Wait for pupillary response; if slow, ensure no residual OVD is blocking receptors.
Step 5: Verify the pupil is round and central without iris incarceration in the wound.

content.explanation: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis. Though rare with intraocular use, systemic absorption can occur through the nasolacrimal duct.

sections.title: CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATIONS
content: Active Anterior Uveitis: Risk of synechiae formation and increased inflammation.
Neovascular Glaucoma: Risk of bleeding from fragile iris vessels.
Malignant Glaucoma: May worsen the anterior displacement of the lens-iris diaphragm.
Known Hypersensitivity to Acetylcholine or Carbachol.
Asthma/COPD: Extreme caution due to risk of bronchospasm from systemic absorption.

sections.title: Differential: Causes of Poor Pupillary Response

rows: Physical barrier prevents drug reaching M3 receptors
Damage to sphincter muscle (e.g., prior acute glaucoma)

sections.title: Ocular Complications & Side Effects
content: Postoperative 'Brow Ache': Ciliary muscle spasm (common with Carbachol).
Corneal Edema: Rare, linked to preservatives or pH imbalance in non-buffered solutions.
Retinal Detachment: Historically debated link due to peripheral retinal traction from ciliary body contraction.
Anterior Chamber Inflammation: Increased protein flare due to breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier.
Induced Myopia: Temporary shift due to ciliary contraction (accommodative spasm).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check the dual-chamber vial for Miochol-E; ensure the center stopper has fallen and the drug is fully dissolved.
Carbachol (Miostat) is significantly more potent and is the drug of choice for lowering IOP after a complicated case.
During PKP, miosis is vital to avoid 'cheese-wiring' the donor tissue with the iris during suturing.
Avoid miotics if you suspect you will need to re-enter the eye for a posterior segment complication (miosis obscures the view).

sections.title: The Role of Carbachol in Glaucoma
sections.content: Carbachol is often preferred in glaucoma filtration surgery or complex cataract cases with high risk of postoperative IOP spikes. Unlike Acetylcholine, which is rapidly degraded, Carbachol provides sustained miosis and trabecular meshwork tension for up to 24 hours, effectively blunting the 4-6 hour post-op pressure rise.

sections.title: Management of Miotic-Induced Spasm
content: Step 1: Patient complains of severe headache or ocular pain post-op.
Step 2: Assess IOP to rule out pressure spike.
Step 3: If IOP is normal, diagnose ciliary spasm.
Step 4: Use mild cycloplegics (e.g., Cyclopentolate) if severe.
Step 5: Counsel patient on the transient nature of the symptoms.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Preservative-Free Formulations
content: Move toward single-dose, preservative-free (PF) formulations to eliminate TASS (Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome) risk.
Studies comparing intracameral miotics vs. topical instillations show 30% faster onset with the intracameral route.
Development of sustained-release miosis/mydriasis combinations for complex vitreoretinal-anterior segment combined cases.
